## Persistence and recovery limits

- Linux, its temporary home and unsaved drafts live in browser RAM. Reload,
  closing the tab, browser/OS failure or End session can lose them. Explicitly
  download/export work or save it in My server files. No VM snapshot/autosave is
  promised. The host filesystem is not exposed to the guest.
- Registered users have private UUID-based disk folders and separate authoritative
  login/permission services. Explicit server-file saves survive refresh/sign-in.
  Anonymous visitors have no server folder. Sign-in keeps the existing Linux VM
  and offers the private volume; it does not upload temporary files automatically.
- Browser caching holds verified public code/boot assets, not identities, private
  documents or API responses. Persistence permission can be denied; the current
  test received false. Clearing site storage rebuilds public assets from server.
- A transient connection loss blocks website controls while preserving the same
  living tab/VM. Recovery cannot prevent browser Reload/Close or an OS killing
  the tab. After a reload, the cached shell honestly warns that old RAM is gone.
- Public routed groups have3–8fixed members, a controller and at most300-second
  leases. No dynamic membership, controller failover or group renewal is promised.
  All participants can read public-group messages. Browser peer chat remains
  available to anonymous identities; Linux Internet requires registration.
- Recovery is bounded and RAM-only:64cached originals/1MiB charged cache;
  originals expire within60seconds; at most16items/request, four shared repair
  jobs and a five-second absolute request deadline. Expired, unavailable or
  oversized gaps remain visibly incomplete. Recovered chat is marked historical;
  it cannot trigger game moves. No permanent chat history or consensus claim.
- The shared networking allowance defaults to128MiB per desktop tab, configurable
 32..1024MiB. It is accounting, not reserved physical RAM or a browser-wide cap.
  Full gossip/islands, chunked durable checkpoints, PoW and8k test execution remain
  future work. See the latest ROADMAP.md section.

## What does not work / is not finished

- Public production login/identity is NOT enabled or security-approved. Dedicated
  service isolation, complete request/load/proxy review, recovery/backup/rotation,
  abuse/retention policy and independent review remain open.
- No measured independent-network/WAN connectivity. All recent Chrome relay,
  shared-port and discovery evidence is on this host with disposable TLS fixtures.
  SPKI/fixture-CA exceptions do not prove public certificate trust.
- No deployed public TURN, public 443 multiplexing, router/DNS changes or reviewed
  production credential/egress/allocation policy. No promise that only 443 will
  suffice on every visitor network. TURN expiry is not instant allocation revocation.
- Multiparty public room membership/routed forwarding is unimplemented. Existing
  grants explicitly bind two participants to one connection; do not remove that
  guard without a new verified admission profile and actual three-peer evidence.
- Private group crypto, key epochs, routed private messages and large-scale
  distributed routing remain gated/unimplemented. No scale claim follows from models.
- No complete history repair. Reordered chat has bounded replay protection and
  incomplete-history warnings; chess gaps freeze the legal prefix.
- Ordinary Chrome cannot expose raw ICMP/Ethernet to a website. Using each
  visitor's own connection for arbitrary guest ping still needs a native helper
  or modified browser. Guest relay Internet currently exits the relay host.
- The complete stack has not yet been proven in ONE execution combining
  discovery + session-issued TURN/TLS + guest Internet + support restart.
  Separate overlapping integration runs passed; do not combine them into a
  stronger claim.

## Gateway/access-control layer APPROVED and important — user direction

The user explicitly approved the gateway/access-control layer as a core
requirement. They want controlled internal AND external resources: selected
internal read-only file shares, selected websites, access rules and speed/usage
limits per user/use. This extends the active networking/identity objective;
keep /desktop unchanged and do functional work only in active-system/hidden.
No specific private folder, internal host or recipient account has been chosen.
Do not expose a host filesystem or open general LAN access without that mapping.

Implementation direction: a managed default-deny resource policy with narrow
explicit service exceptions, independently enforced host egress restrictions,
a read-only file broker (server-side permission enforcement, never trust client
read-only flags), and identity-bound quotas/rate queues keyed by stable account
subject and resource. Anonymous sessions need separate caps; do not claim they
are reliable per-person identity or that reconnecting must reset account quotas.
Current global Origin+guest-cookie gate is NOT identity-bound and must be
extended before claiming per-user gateway enforcement. Current TrafficBudget
terminates excess traffic; smooth speed control requires real pacing/backpressure.

Website/path/method controls need an application proxy/broker; raw IP/port rules
cannot distinguish all virtual hosts or enforce read-only file operations.
Keep private LAN and own WAN address blocked for raw guest access, and expose
selected internal shares through the broker with only the approved root/actions.
Read-only protects originals; downloaded copies remain editable by the visitor.
Browser-local computation and ordinary new tabs do not pass through this gateway.

## Registered-user persistent folders approved; Linux account question

The user explicitly requested save/write access with ONE UNIQUE PRIVATE SERVER
FOLDER PER REGISTERED ACCOUNT, NONE FOR ANY ANONYMOUS USER. Preserve temporary
browser/v86 files for anonymous users; never allocate an anonymous server home
or grant anonymous persistent-save rights. This authorizes controlled personal
storage for active-system, not changes to /desktop or a blanket mapping of host
home directories. Shared read-only resources have separate explicit ACLs.

Use the existing persistent web-account subject (user:UUID), not a client-chosen
username/path, guest Linux UID or session ID, for each personal storage namespace.
Same account on another device/session reuses its folder. Per-user quotas must
also use stable account subject across sessions. Personal files are private from
other accounts. Write/create/update and quota enforcement happen on the server;
client-visible read-only/hidden buttons are never authorization. Safe atomic
saves, content/version preconditions, traversal/symlink/hardlink refusal and
storage/transfer quotas are required. Anonymous certificates must fail before
any server-folder creation. No actual private share path has been selected.

User asked whether Linux accounts could handle usernames/passwords. Recommended
reusing the already implemented web accounts/password hashes and mapping their
stable subject to storage. Host Linux service accounts enforce process/storage
boundaries. Browser v86 Linux is visitor-controlled and is NOT an identity
authority. Linux PAM could integrate existing host accounts, but does not remove
web-session/resource-policy/quota work and is not needed for these public web
registrations. Existing server code uses salted Argon2id password hashes in
private SQLite state. Do not copy passwords into guest Linux or create host
interactive logins for website registrants as an unrequested convenience.
No identity migration to PAM has been requested or implemented.

Local gateway WIP started: gateway_service/__init__.py, policy.py and files.py.
Policy is a strict operator-owned resource allowlist with ACL/limits, pinned
HTTP destination IPs, explicit private-address exceptions for brokered HTTP,
own-WAN refusal and read-only file roots disjoint from private/control trees.
ReadOnlyShare uses descriptor-relative O_NOFOLLOW/O_RDONLY and refuses links,
special files and traversal. These files are UNTESTED AND NOT EXPORTED/DEPLOYED.
They currently implement only read-only file/http policy primitives. Do not claim
personal save, quota accounting, signed gateway grants, file HTTP service, OS
egress firewall or per-user guest network enforcement exists yet. Next build
identity-bound one-use authorization, durable quota/pacing, registered personal
storage, broker transport, native lifecycle/firewall and UI integration.

Planned issuer integration should keep credential checking in the existing
issuer and resource access in a separate gateway role. A dedicated gateway
identity-confirmation endpoint can reuse live session/key/account-generation
checks and sign short-lived, request/nonce-bound confirmations; gateway applies
its own ACLs and verifies client proof. This avoids trusting detached browser
Linux users or granting general LAN access. Preserve disabled-account semantics
and explicitly bound any in-flight authorization lifetime. Issuer restart
resilience remains unfinished and matters for long-lived gateway access.

## Device-local saved-account revision floor — 2026-10-26

The source AccountLinks service now stores issuer/account, highest revision and
SHA-256 in a strict IndexedDB transaction (`codi-account-link-floor-v1`). It
checks on read and before/after file writes, rejects older/missing/different
same-revision files and corrupt/unavailable local records, and stops automatic

## Same-profile account change propagation — 2026-10-26

Account-link service floor transactions now send a small same-origin
BroadcastChannel hint after a committed version change. The hint contains the
account key only, never contacts or grants. The receiving session immediately
blocks new automatic introductions, cancels non-ready owned introductions and
keeps ready peers. It re-reads the existing authenticated account file and
checks the strict browser floor before applying any list. A stale in-flight
read is rejected; an untrusted hint cannot add a contact. If the server may
have committed a write but the writer's local floor or response failed, a
best-effort hint is still sent, including after the writer signs out; receivers
still trust only their own authenticated read and local floor.

One session-owned refresh job/timer coalesces hints. Automatic account-file
reads are at least five seconds apart using a monotonic clock; a frozen account
does not repeatedly fetch. Signout clears its scheduled timer and closes the
observer. On visibility/pageshow/resume, an observed floor is checked locally
to catch a missed hint; an unchanged floor does not trigger an HTTP read.
Browser suspension, unavailable BroadcastChannel, direct file edits outside
AccountLinks and other profiles/devices can delay or miss active notification.
New or cleared profiles still lack an account-wide authoritative rollback floor.

## Compact private file version — 2026-10-26

Source-only gateway `version` operation returns just byte length and SHA-256
for an authenticated personal file, using the existing read permission, exact
request schema, private directory checks, quotas and no-store response. The
client validates bounded size, canonical hash and exact response fields. This
provides a bandwidth-saving primitive for future cross-device change detection;
it does not notify, poll, establish an account-wide rollback floor or authorize
contacts. The server currently reads the whole bounded file to hash it.
`gateway-version-check.py` exercises real issuer/gateway proofs, replacement,
isolation, read revocation and anonymous refusal; the client check rejects
malformed responses. The change is not installed or deployed. Older gateways
will reject this operation; clients must negotiate availability before use.
Do not enable polling without bounding its issuer/gateway request load and
accounting for mobile data, failure, device suspension and stale state.


## Cross-device version polling candidate — 2026-10-26

Source-only host now optionally checks the compact file version every five
minutes per signed-in session while the page is visible and automatic account
discovery is ready. It runs only if `gateway.fileVersionChecks === true`; the
current managed issuer does not advertise this capability. The watcher is
session-owned, has at most one check, and is cancelled on session retirement.
A changed hash blocks new introductions and invokes the ordinary authenticated
file read and durable device-local revision/hash checks; it is never a grant.
Errors block introductions until a later verified reload; existing connections
are not revoked. A delayed check after page suspension can leave information
stale. Different-device notification is therefore eventual and contingent on
visibility, network, and continued operation, not instantaneous or proven WAN.
The gateway currently authenticates each check using multiple requests and its
existing tight admission limit, so this is not an 8k-scale notification design;
measure and redesign/cap before broad enablement. A distinct authoritative
account-wide rollback floor and server recovery remain unfinished.

Four-validator longer first-grant observation — 2026-10-26: source-only `member-four-validator-small-quota-r2-result.json` PASS6 in 177.884 seconds with eight local Chrome identities, four validators (quorum three), a full initial seed and a real 4096-byte/2-second newcomer download quota. Signed outbound newcomer payload measured from bind through grant: credit grants 130,571 bytes/139 frames; replica `get` 125,084 bytes/121 frames; `node` calls 36,130 bytes/24 frames; scout 23,385 bytes/6 frames; credit requests 21,134 bytes/24 frames; head calls 9,783 bytes/7 frames; acknowledgments 7,151 bytes/8 frames; bind 2,216 bytes/1 frame. Many individual chunk requests and per-request credits dominate; repeated scout/head attempts contribute. Investigate the early generic refusal and improve batching/credit efficiency without weakening quota reservations, ACL rechecks, compatibility, or cancellation. Search-start is verified, but a completed alternative path is not asserted by this test. Live chat remains paused.

## Verified bounded checkpoint gap fill — 2026-10-27

Source-only archive `fillCheckpointGap` replays a complete ascending batch of signed blocks from the retained pre-checkpoint position to the current accepted head. It validates transitions, stages content-addressed history, compares the final state and head, and atomically replaces the history pin without changing pending originals. It requires the entire gap (maximum 256 blocks, 8 MiB input) in one call; it does not fetch from peers or run automatically, and larger gaps need resumable chunked work. Existing current-head conflict, storage permission, capacity and timeout protections apply. The history API remains responsible for reporting any other missing older data.

Real local Chrome `device-checkpoint-gap-fill-r2-result.json` PASS (81 checks): includes rejecting partial or invalid histories, actual IndexedDB transaction abort without floor/pending/accounting changes, filling a 69-block gap including a post-checkpoint block, preserving a pending signed original, paging back to the older block, and reopening the archive. Four logical keys in one browser; no peer transfer or WAN test for this method. First run r1 failed on a duplicate fixture variable before execution; retained as evidence. No production deployment or live-chat enablement.

## Bounded peer checkpoint-gap transfer — 2026-10-27

Source-only `DeviceChannelTransfer.stageCheckpointGap` fetches hash-checked content nodes over the authorized member connection, reconstructs a bounded batch of signed blocks, and passes it to the archive's full transition replay. `DeviceMemberChannel.fillCheckpointGap` and the desktop channel facade expose this explicitly. The peer must currently offer exactly the reader's accepted height/head; the whole gap is limited to 256 blocks and 8 MiB of block input, is assembled in memory, and is committed atomically. It does not automatically select peers, follow a peer beyond the local head, recover gaps larger than the bound, or provide resumable block-level completion. Scratch content is unaccepted and subject to existing quotas; completion attempts to remove its scratch job.

`member-checkpoint-gap-rtc-r2-result.json` PASS (36 checks): four separate local Chrome profiles and real RTCDataChannels; one actual validator, reader checkpoint at height 22 after retaining height 3, 19-block history fill from an authorized peer, unchanged accepted head and exact blocked pending signed original, and history pages connecting to retained older blocks. The earlier r1 passed but its driver was edited during the run; r2 is the authoritative repeat. Live chat stays disabled; no deployment.

## History repair from a newer peer — 2026-10-27

The member gap-fill path now accepts an authorized peer ahead of the reader. It walks bounded newest-first ancestry pages (at most 8,192 certificates), verifies every quorum certificate and parent link back to the reader's already accepted head, checks the content-addressed locator there, then fetches and replays the still-bounded gap. A peer behind the reader or a conflicting certified chain is refused; the archive still independently validates and atomically commits replay. This does not automatically select peers, resume larger than 256-block gaps, or independently test 8,192 certificates at scale.

`member-checkpoint-gap-ahead-rtc-r1-result.json` PASS (37 checks): four local Chrome profiles, real RTCDataChannels, one validator. ## Automatic bounded history repair — 2026-10-27

Member maintenance now notices an installed checkpoint gap and, when it is at most 256 blocks and reading is authorized, attempts repair with one connected member at a time. Failed attempts rotate through the current peers and use exponential delay from 30 seconds to at most five minutes; the accepted floor and pending originals remain authoritative. Maintenance reports `member-history-incomplete` when no pending original takes precedence. This is background work, is bounded by the existing peer/data/cache controls, and remains limited to an 8 MiB complete batch; it is not resumable larger-gap recovery or proven low-data optimization. Gap attempts with no peers wait for normal topology wakeup. Retry state is in-memory and resets on reopen.

`member-checkpoint-gap-auto-rtc-r1-result.json` PASS (38 checks), four local Chrome profiles with actual RTC and one validator: a test-injected first provider failure was followed after the retry delay by a different provider, automatic history repair joined the old history and preserved the exact blocked pending original. Live chat remains disabled and no deployment occurred.

## Incremental history recovery — 2026-10-27

Archive history repair now accepts an ascending verified segment, replays every transition, proves the resulting intermediate boundary against the already accepted checkpoint, and atomically stores that boundary and reconstructed history while preserving the accepted head, operation tree and pending originals. Subsequent segments resume from the persisted boundary; the last segment reconnects the complete history. The member transfer retrieves up to 64 blocks or 8 MiB per batch (whichever comes first), and maintenance can continue an incomplete gap up to the existing 8,192-certificate proof bound. Content is bounded, but locating each batch currently walks the history from the offered head again, so long gaps may use excessive bandwidth and need locator optimization before large-scale/limited-data claims.

`device-checkpoint-gap-partial-r1-result.json` PASS (83 checks): partial commit, close/reopen, final recovery, pending retention, invalid inputs and actual native transaction abort. ## Resumable automatic checkpoint ancestry — 2026-10-27

## Channel creation and joining functions — 2026-10-28

User clarified channel types: official server-created channels keep participant device copies, prefer peer-to-peer transfers, and use a server-disk history copy as fallback. User-created channels keep history on participant devices; server history hosting requires explicit opt-in. These policies are separate from the temporary introduction coordinator. User requested underlying functions first, no GUI redesign.

Working source `assets/desktop/device-channel-session.mjs` adds `createChannelInvitation(channel)` and `joinChannelInvitation(invitation, peerId)` on the existing shared channel view. Join validates the signed policy and a connected membership-capable peer before creating an actor, restores an existing saved actor when available, and reports `searching` separately from a bound `connected` transport. A bound result does not by itself promise that history has caught up or the user has write permission. The shared session continues to own storage and peer connections; no GUI was added. These additions are source-only, not in the live release.

## Channel moderation direction — 2026-10-28

User wants IRC-like controls over users and channels; the operator controls official channels and creators control their own, while game channel controls are defined and enforced by the game. Official channel server backing should remain available as a fallback while participants prefer P2P; the server may bootstrap small channels, but no hard size-based switch should be assumed. User-created channel history remains device-backed absent explicit server opt-in.

Source-only `setChannelMemberAccess(channel,subject,{read,write})` exposes the existing signed permission queue through the shared channel view, rejects non-chat/game streams and malformed access, and relies on the existing controller authorization and accepted channel history. It acts on a device channel actor key, not yet an account-wide identity or platform ban. A returned operation is pending until accepted. `device-channel-control-compiled-r2-result.json` PASS10 with two actual local Chrome profiles and manual RTC: invitation/join/history/reply, controller queues a read/write revocation accepted into channel history, and non-controller cannot moderate. `device-channel-control-state-r1-result.json` PASS62 separately verifies the existing cryptographic state transition refuses operations after revocation, but is one-browser fixture scope. Initial moderation r1 test had a wait predicate that incorrectly treated a missing permission row as revoked; r2 corrected it. No live deployment, automatic join, server-level account/channel bans, creator delegation, timed bans, kick, game-specific moderation or GUI. Offline peers can temporarily have stale permissions, and received content cannot be erased from devices. Continue the underlying channel creation/join and official server fallback work alongside proper signed account-bound moderation, scope, authorization, revocation recovery and game rules.

User narrowed moderation: ban registered accounts for now; anonymous-network shutdown is acceptable if anonymous traffic is abused. Do not present device-key revocation as an account ban. Existing `origin_service.lifecycle.set_disabled` is an operator-only platform account disable with generation-based session invalidation; it blocks sign-in and renewal but an already issued identity certificate retains its validity until expiry and cannot be retroactively erased from disconnected peers. It is not a creator-controlled per-channel account ban. Channel bans need verified issuer/subject-to-device binding for every device and signed account-scoped channel policy and revocation, with offline consistency limits. No anonymous-network kill switch was implemented or verified in this turn.

Device chess match composition — 2026-10-28: live manifest `ebce1681dc50bbd60cb3dad164cbe952cc9d3a362a19d4e5277336b6ffea36e3`, box-git source `5f2f50c`. Rooms now offers a text-based match flow: players create device-owned public player identifiers, White creates a game and separate spectator chat, and shares a public match code. Spectators join without a player key. Match shortcuts are stored in localStorage scoped to the device-history identity; channel keys, messages and accepted game history remain in the existing permitted device stores. Saved match can reopen after browser restart. User must exchange Black's public player identifier before creation. Shared service creates and validates the separate policies; legal moves are prechecked against the current board and independently revalidated by the accepted-history protocol; pending remains explicitly pending. The invitation contains both public policy wires but is not itself a signed binding between them. Created game still has White as its only validator, so Black cannot rely on acceptance while White is offline; no joint validator or independent island liveness claim. Game/chat creation is two operations, not an atomic transaction.

Signed spam marks with expandable originals — 2026-10-28: active release `2790f3d7dfded55e4f0b40290d63c292ce102af4491f288cd61eacfbc9efa488`, box-git source `cbad6ee`. Channel owner can select a message and queue a signed `moderation` operation (`action:spam`); accepted history records the message ID, owner key and index. Other channel members verify and replicate that accepted operation. The conversation shows an inline collapsed details element, labeled “marked as spam by you” for the owner and “marked as spam by channel owner” for others; opening it exposes the original text. The original remains in participant history/storage; a mark is not a deletion and cannot erase copies. Existing display/snapshot is bounded to the recent 64 messages; displaying originals beyond that window and account display-name attribution are unfinished. Only the channel creator key can issue marks, not delegated moderators; account bans and official-channel moderation remain open. Duplicate marks are rejected. New moderation operation and optional snapshot field are backward-compatible for older unmarked histories but older software cannot validate new moderation records; no old clients were retained per user test-site direction. Marks have a bounded 16,384-entry snapshot allowance and no unmark operation yet; invalid/saturated marks may remain pending and require future UX handling.

Multiple simultaneous matches and author spam marks — 2026-10-28: active live manifest `a29f412cd8bf7e137e052d953e017b0595088b3cdc3123ffaa71f641639e0cca`, source/box-git `78b9408`. Rooms supports three named matches in three windows, each with independent game and chat. Local saved-match shortcuts update across same-document windows and cross-tab storage events; Web Locks serialize updates where supported (fallback without Web Locks does not guarantee cross-tab atomicity). ## Rolling channel discovery groundwork — 2026-10-28

User wants automatically listed user channels, official/user labels, a rolling event stream with bounded browser memory, and per-user configurable retention including never delete. Signed exports should preserve verification material; current device private keys are nonextractable and private-key backup requires separate design. Do not remove history until catch-up/checkpoint and replica retention safety are designed. Browser quotas still apply.

Source-only groundwork: `network/channel-listing.mjs` signs and validates user listings against the owner and channel policy and provides a bounded recent in-memory index. `steward/channel_index.py` independently validates the same signed policy and listing and maintains a bounded, expiring, cursor-addressed in-memory feed. Neither module is wired to the steward WebSocket protocol, browser publishing, discovery UI, deployment, or an official-channel authority. The feed is metadata only, and not a saved chat service. Tests: `scripts/fixtures/channel-listing-check.mjs` (Node, 10 checks) and `scripts/fixtures/channel-index-server-check.py` (Python, 11 checks) pass. These tests do not prove a network stream, joining from search, WAN behavior, retention, signed export, or account backup. Next connect authenticated publication and bounded streaming/replay with ordered events, backpressure, and reconnect behavior, then publish automatically and integrate discovery UI; test interoperability and actual independent-network use before claiming completion.

Follow-up: `INDEX_PUBLISH` and cursor-paged `INDEX_READ` are now present in the authenticated steward protocol and validated in `network/support-client.mjs`; state is scoped to the lease's public scope, volatile and bounded, with a random feed epoch to detect restart. `network/channel-index-stream.mjs` adds bounded browser replay, retry scheduling, owner-signed description publication and cleanup, but is not yet hooked to the desktop or the UI. The current transport uses bounded polling, not pushed events. Local mock-browser stream checks and direct protocol checks pass; neither proves actual WebSocket interoperability. User requested simple search/list/join and owner-editable description. Implement automatic listing, persistent owner description and the simple UI, then verify actual browser-to-steward and WAN operation. Export public keys and signatures, not private keys.

Directory follow-up: owner descriptions now use a backward-compatible optional field in the transactional device channel directory, with exact-version update and cross-tab notification. The preliminary channel UI saves the description and refreshes the selected owned channel listing every 90 seconds while that window is open. It does not yet renew all owned channels in the background, and index entries expire when not refreshed. `ChannelIndexStream` is exported via the shared history service and the service was compiled successfully at `.build/shared-services/channel-index-r1`; this alone does not validate the full release packaging or actual browser behavior. UI/service integration is source-only and must be tested with real IndexedDB and the upgraded steward before deployment. Old steward deployments do not support INDEX requests, so avoid serving this client against them until coordinated rollout. Public listing history remains volatile metadata; no official-server history implemented here.

This is local only, not independent WAN or deployed. Two earlier failed receipts are test corrections: r1 had malformed JavaScript selector and r2 used a potentially unchanged test UUID. The previous debug-r1 failure used different accounts in one browser profile, causing its first account session to be replaced; r3 of that debug test passed with independent profiles. User clarified that channel peers should gossip temporary signed connection introductions so known channel participants can connect without relying on a central server; a new or returning participant still needs a saved reachable peer or introduction fallback. Inspect existing `network/device-member-introductions.mjs` and its admission, expiry, bounded routing and reconnect handling before changing it; do not put long-lived credentials in public listings. WebTransport request was withdrawn: retain WebRTC for peer connectivity.

Official-channel metadata registry foundation (local, not wired or deployed): `steward/official_registry.py` stores explicitly operator-enrolled channel IDs, signed policy and genesis pin, display metadata and enabled state in SQLite. Initial test exposed that ECDSA re-signing identical policy yields a different wire; registry now compares the signed-content genesis hash and retains the original wire. This is metadata only, has no operator authentication/API, history storage, server fallback, P2P preference or official UI, and must not be presented as working official channels. Next integrate a protected operator-controlled enrollment path and implement a pinned, verified durable replica and fallback that cannot accept user-channel histories absent explicit opt-in.

Official scratch foundation (local, unconnected): the same registry now accepts bounded SHA-256-addressed scratch bytes only for enrolled, enabled official channels, with a configurable per-channel allowance (default 64 MiB), atomic idempotent insert, no overwrite, and inaccessible scratch while disabled. These are deliberately **unverified scratch bytes**, not accepted history or a server fallback; no network API exposes them. The store does not yet check node structure, channel-scoped DAG, signatures, authority, completeness or concurrent operational isolation beyond the SQLite transaction. Implement verified promotion and authorization before any serving, and separately implement operator controls and browser fallback. No live changes.

Experimental genesis-only public-chat replay `steward/official_chat_replay.py` (local, unconnected): validates pinned signed public-read/public-write chat policy, certificate, ancestry, operation commitment, signed author sequence, replay witness and resulting state hash for chat-only blocks. Experimental replay now additionally supports owner-issued message/author spam marks and non-account-linked read/write permission changes, enforcing owner, conditional head, validator read, permission revision, and denied writes. `.build/checks/official-browser-moderation-replay-r1.json` PASS9 on two browsers with actual signed message and author marks; `.build/checks/official-browser-permission-replay-r1.json` PASS10 adds an owner-issued write revocation, confirms the affected browser cannot queue chat, and compares Python replay with the exact browser state. Experimental account replay: `steward/official_chat_replay.py` now handles account-linked device grants and account block/unblock with owner checks, pinned subject binding, blocked-account denial, validator protection and permission revision. `.build/checks/official-browser-account-replay-r1.json` PASS10 with four actual browser profiles, real local registered identity service, two device keys for one account, observer, signed block/unblock and exact Python-vs-browser final state/head. Experimental in-process incremental replay: `ExperimentalChatReplay` now owns its state from verified genesis and accepts consecutive batches of at most 64 blocks, cloning the current floor and committing only after the entire batch verifies. Public snapshots are copies and there is no method to load a caller-provided floor. `.build/checks/official-browser-incremental-replay-r2.json` PASS15 using two actual browser-generated blocks: separate single-block appends match full/browser replay; mutating a snapshot cannot alter internal state; invalid next block leaves the floor untouched; a batch containing a valid block then invalid block leaves the entire batch uncommitted. This only removes the per-process total limit conceptually; >64 real blocks, durability/restart, multi-process concurrency, full policy/canonicalization parity, and secure atomic persistence remain untested/unimplemented. No live deployment or accepted-history fallback.

Experimental durable block replay (local, unconnected): `OfficialChannelRegistry` now stores replayed block wires transactionally after replaying every retained block from genesis, validating a caller-provided expected head and verifying the next batch. Experimental official-channel restoration: an opt-in session lookup rechecks the current same-origin directory for each restored channel, verifies the signed policy and saved genesis, restores its official history pin, and wakes recovery; temporary lookup failures retry with bounded exponential backoff. Lookup is opt-in and has not been enabled or deployed on the live site. UI, production provisioning, independent-network proof and the rest of the goal remain unfinished.

## Current peer recovery and corruption check — 2026-10-28

`.build/checks/current-gap-crash-r4.json` PASS38: four local Chromium profiles, five launches, actual RTC, one validator and reduced eight-block fixture batches. A reader commits a partial verified recovery, is killed after the durable boundary, restores its pending original, and automatically completes peer history recovery. The fixture now compares the offered verified head instead of assuming at least two ancestry pages; actual batching can return one. This is local and not a WAN, large-scale or power-loss proof.

`scripts/member-segment-head-chain-corruption-check.py` and its fallback companion were updated to open all enclosing permission controls and compare the verified ancestry head rather than a fixed page count. Corruption rerun `.build/checks/current-head-corruption-r4.json` FAIL at check 22: corruption injection occurred (`poisonStillPending=false`) but the pull returned successfully and the reader reached height 7, contrary to the older fixture expectation that the whole pull must fail at height 3. Current `#readContent` verifies each content response and tries other eligible peers after invalid data; this behavior is consistent with successful fallback but the fixture does not yet identify and prove the clean alternative response, nor independently verify that the accepted history matches the provider after the injection. Do not call this a corruption-rejection pass. Earlier r1 failed at the closed permission controls and r2 at the stale fixed-page assertion; r3 showed the same later failure without the added injection diagnostics. No product or deployment change in these runs; fixture cleanup reported no error. Next instrument which peer supplies the rejected and accepted responses, prove the resulting accepted head against the authorized provider, and exercise all-providers-corrupt rejection separately.

Corruption follow-up `.build/checks/current-head-corruption-r7.json` PASS34 with four local browsers and RTC: the fixture corrupts every attempted head-chain reply and checks that the saved head does not advance; after the 15-second bad-peer quarantine expires, it corrupts one reply, records a clean response for the same requested history from a different peer, and verifies the recovered accepted head against the original provider's recorded signed head. The rest of the history and revocation checks pass and fixture cleanup reports no error. This tests injected head-chain corruption, not every possible malformed frame, WAN, or large meshes. r5 failed an intermittent mismatch check; r6 passed the single-corrupt case after retrying only the explicit earlier-durable-work condition. No live deployment.

Concurrency finding: `DeviceReplicaScheduler` has at most two active automatic channel tasks per session; `DeviceChannelSession.#work` holds a per-channel `working` guard for the duration of its asynchronous job, and automatic work checks that guard. Native Web Crypto and network calls are asynchronous, but channel logic is not currently isolated in dedicated Web Workers. Long channel jobs may delay same-channel operations, and two long jobs may delay other channels. Investigate finer-grained safe commit coordination, worker offload where profiling justifies it, fairness and bounded resource use, with multi-channel responsiveness and recovery tests before changing live behavior. Preserve ordered durable state and authorization checks.

Queue fairness/resource investigation: `.build/checks/submission-wait-flood-network-r2.json` PASS5 using three actual local RTC browsers and a fixture-held validator handler: one bound peer sent repeated valid relayed requests and occupied two actual queue slots; a direct probe could still acquire one `consensusJobs` slot at that moment, and waiters drained after release. It did NOT prove full exhaustion or another real channel's failure. Source inspection shows `DeviceReplicaExchange` counts incoming member submissions against the shared `consensusJobs` budget and lane limit (4), the same pool used by validator protocol requests, so waiting requests consume slots while idle; this creates a real fairness/deadlock concern under saturation and makes the prior synthetic separate-channel result insufficient. Do not deploy queue candidate until tested under actual multi-channel/multi-validator saturation and appropriately isolated/fair resources or a justified bounded reserve. Flood r1 waited for three queue entries, did not observe three before its deadline and then hung during failure cleanup because the release hook was mistakenly called on c instead of a; process/session was still running at handoff. Test scripts now release a's held hook on exceptions; r2 passed/cleaned. No production changes, prior live remains unchanged. Next investigate separate member-submission budget or carefully reserved capacity, preserve bounded memory/cancellation and avoid deadlock; verify using real simultaneous network requests and another active channel, not only synthetic lock jobs.

Experimental resource-lane isolation: `network/resource-budget.mjs` adds bounded `memberSubmitJobs:4` with independently accounted leases; `network/device-replica-exchange.mjs` assigns member `submit`/`relay-submit` RPCs to that lane, keeping validator consensus and member-control/repair lanes separate. Test-only `.build/shared-services/submission-lane-network-probe-r1` patches the pinned live candidate's exchange classifier and exposes queue count; local browser fixture imports the edited actual `network/resource-budget.mjs`. `.build/checks/submission-lane-isolation-r1.json` PASS7: three actual RTC browsers, four member-submit slots occupied by one active + three waiting requests; observed memberSubmitJobs=4, consensusJobs=0, and a second channel committed a real message while those slots were saturated. `.build/checks/submission-lane-multivalidator-burst-r1.json` PASS7 (four validators/quorum3, six local browsers, three concurrent writes), `.build/checks/submission-lane-revocation-r1.json` PASS8 (actual queued request rejected after signed write revocation). Not deployed: the live networking runtime owns the `ResourceBudget`, so BOTH its served module/package and shared-service candidate must be updated together; older runtime would reject `memberSubmitJobs`. Need exact release packaging and live-compatible tests plus one-peer fairness: a single peer filled all 4 message-submit slots (preserving consensus does not guarantee other members can submit). Avoid premature deployment; no broad scaling, independent WAN or latency proof. Prior flood r1 finally ended FAIL (expected timeout), owned profiles/fixture removed but browser cleanup recorded timeout; r2 and new tests cleaned successfully.

Member submission fairness experiment: `network/device-replica-exchange.mjs` now locally admits at most two simultaneous incoming `memberSubmitJobs` per authenticated transport peer, after checking its channel binding. Existing receive error handling immediately replies `unavailable` for excess; this is an in-flight job bound, not a data/download allowance. Test-only `.build/shared-services/submission-fair-network-probe-r1` patches exact live-based candidate service classifier and limit and exposes wait count; browser fixture imports edited `network/resource-budget.mjs`. `.build/checks/submission-fair-network-r1.json` PASS5 real local RTC: one peer holds an inbound job and sends two extra identical signed requests; validator records per-peer refusal, a second directly connected peer enters the real wait queue, and both original messages reach all three browsers exactly once. `.build/checks/submission-fair-ten-r1.json` PASS4 ten local browsers/three simultaneous authors/same verified head, and `submission-fair-multi-r1.json` PASS7 six local browsers/four validators/quorum3/three simultaneous originals; both ran concurrently, not performance comparisons or independent WAN. Per-peer means multiple authors routed through one relay share its two slots, so test relay congestion and retry/fairness with multiple authors before deployment; rotating identities/connections can still bypass the per-peer cap, and queue has no strict FIFO fairness. The lane change requires paired release of live networking resource-budget and shared service; existing test-only wrappers are not deployable and live remains unchanged. Next build a narrowly pinned paired service/network candidate, run packaged regression and relay-saturation/cancellation/multi-validator failure tests, then test on live only if evidence supports it. Full independent-WAN, durable official channels and chess goal remains open.

## Experimental automatic peer-pending integration — 2026-10-28

Source only, behind `deviceChannels.experimentalPendingSharing === true`; live remains native26-pending-text-r1 and does not offer peer-pending delivery. `network/experimental-pending-gossip.mjs` now periodically exchanges original verified unconfirmed chat proposals over existing authenticated member links, including forwarding received originals, with bounded pages, fanout attempts, retry and per-peer deduplication. `device-channel-session.mjs` creates and closes the inbox and gossip runtime, dispatches pending-share, wakes on new local chat, and exposes a page of peer-pending entries without wires. The Chat view labels peer messages “Unconfirmed from peer,” hides accepted duplicates and collapses messages matching accepted spam marks. The inbox removes accepted entries on read, retains unauthorized entries invisibly, surfaces unexpected corruption/storage errors, and treats an explicitly missing accepted-history node as still-unconfirmed rather than failing the entire snapshot. The channel exchange rechecks both reader permission and original author's write permission on every pending-value chunk and again immediately before transmission. No automatic activation, old-peer feature negotiation, page navigation beyond first 64 in the UI, inbox-capacity backfill, offline validator replacement, independent WAN proof, or release claim.

`.build/checks/pending-peer-automatic-r4.json` PASS13: four local Chromium profiles and explicitly seeded actual RTC links; while sole validator is offline, c→b→d forwards an unconfirmed message and 20 additional messages, verifies no direct c↔d link, renders unconfirmed UI, preserves it across b restart, reconnects and accepts the original, then automatically prunes its inbox copy. Does not assert acceptance of all 20, and does not exercise automatic discovery or independent networks. Earlier r3 found an actual `DeviceArchiveNodeMissing` during recovery: source now handles this as unknown receipt, rather than swallowing all other errors. `.build/checks/pending-peer-automatic-chunk-r1.json` PASS13 with chunk transport and deliberate missing-history injection. `.build/checks/pending-peer-revocation-paged-r3.json` PASS13 and `pending-peer-send-revocation-paged-r2.json` PASS14 cover signed author revocation/regrant and final reader send guard using an explicit fixture-installed adapter and fixture-only handler dispatch override. `.build/checks/pending-peer-chunk-revocation-r1.json` PASS14 holds a real pending-value chunk, updates sender's accepted author permission, then verifies the final chunk guard refuses it; this observes the guard, not independent packet capture. Fixtures explicitly disclose the dispatch override and are not production integration tests. UI, routing and permissions remain experimental until broader lifecycle, scale, interoperability and recovery tests pass.

Follow-up `.build/checks/pending-peer-automatic-r5.json` PASS14: same four-local-browser explicitly seeded topology with 20-message backlog, all 20 subsequently accepted at all four after validator returns; entire test 168.143 seconds, which includes setup, offline relay, restart, reconnect, acceptance and cleanup (not a measured acceptance-only latency). This run used the pre-chunk-guard source copied into its fixture before the guard edit; chunked routing and revoked-author final guard were separately verified in the two subsequent chunk receipts above. These results do not prove ten participants, automatic discovery, external WAN, fast convergence or deployment readiness.

Potential next bottleneck: the member runtime batches a direct validator submission but deliberately selects a single `record` on `relay-submit` (`network/device-member-channel.mjs` maintain and invoke). The r5 writer reaches the validator through b, so its 20-message catch-up cannot use the existing direct-submit batch path. This is a source observation, not a timed isolation proving how much of the 168-second run it caused. Next measure per-stage latency, then design authenticated bounded relay batching with per-original permission/witness/receipt checks, compatibility fallback and tests for partial acceptance and peer failure.

## Experimental relayed submission batches — 2026-10-28

SOURCE ONLY; no live update. `network/device-member-channel.mjs` permits an existing `relay-submit` to carry 2–16 records (max 64 KiB), validates unique signed proposal IDs, common original author and verified author access at every hop, preserves signed authorizations, forwards bounded paths, and has the validator return an individual membership proof for each original. The writer verifies every proof and the checkpoint. An explicit unavailable response to a batch falls back to the original single-record format, allowing old intermediate relays to interoperate; no claim about arbitrary timeouts or every mixed-version topology. A short per-peer exponential retry delay (500 ms, 1 s, then 2 s, bounded map and cleared on success/close) limits repeated unavailable relay attempts. `assets/desktop/device-channel-session.mjs` now supplies traffic-profile batch settings even when automatic peer topology is off; previously that path bypassed batch settings.

## Bounded parallel pending fanout LIVE — 2026-10-28

`ExperimentalPendingGossip` now launches at most four sends in parallel per channel cycle, at most two to one peer, instead of serially waiting up to ten seconds for each. Wakes that arrive during the cycle are retained. This is asynchronous work on the existing browser thread, not a Web Worker; the cycle still waits for all its chosen sends before starting its next cycle, so a hung peer can delay *later* messages for up to the per-send timeout. `pending-peer-slow-neighbor-r1.json` PASS5 with four local browser profiles and manually seeded RTC: one c→b send is held, c→d receives the same signed pending original before release, b receives after release, no accepted-history mutation. `pending-peer-slow-neighbor-compiled-r1.json` PASS5 exact patched service with test-only exports; `pending-peer-slow-neighbor-serial-control-r1.json` intentionally FAILS at 8s waiting for d with fixture-only serial sender, demonstrating the observed bottleneck. `pending-peer-parallel-regression-r1.json` PASS18 multi-hop, restart, 20-message acceptance and batch tampering checks. `pending-peer-seventy-rtc-r1.json` PASS13 four local browsers, actual c→b→d links, sole validator offline: 70 unique pending messages reach d, survive d restart and remain unaccepted. ## Batched peer-pending messages LIVE — 2026-10-28

The authenticated `pending-share` RPC now accepts a bounded batch (2–16 originals, <=64 KiB). Every original is individually signature-verified and authorized at the current verified floor; duplicate IDs reject the batch, the receiver writes new inbox rows and accounting in one strict IDB transaction, and capacity or malformed entries fail without partial inserts. The response identifies each original as unconfirmed/already present/already accepted; no validator authority is conferred. Mixed-author batches recheck all authors and the receiver immediately before initial send and each chunk. An explicit `unavailable` batch response falls back to individual shares with a short per-peer legacy cache; this cannot prove every kind of mixed-version peer/network failure. Fanout groups up to eight originals per peer, bounded to four peer groups; pending multi-page backlogs resume with a 250ms cadence rather than waiting four seconds per page. No full worker-thread isolation, pull-based chunk reconciliation, full inbox backfill, or 8k proof.

`pending-peer-batch-security-r2.json` PASS11 real local RTC with fixture-installed adapter, idempotence, invalid/duplicate atomic refusal and capacity refusal. `pending-peer-batch-legacy-r1.json` PASS4 runtime fixture simulates a legacy single-only peer and confirms fallback. `pending-peer-batch-chunk-revocation-r1.json` PASS14 holds a real chunk of a mixed-author batch; sender learns that one author lost write access and final transmit guard refuses it. ## Offline author signed-record experiment — 2026-10-28

SOURCE ONLY; live remains native26-peer-batch-r1. `network/experimental-authorized-pending.mjs` validates a peer-authored chat original and its separate signer-bound operation authorization, current local reader/author rights and policy pins, then can explicitly submit it to a bound validator and verify the validator checkpoint and membership receipt. `assets/desktop/authorized-pending-store.mjs` is a separate consent-gated strict IndexedDB prototype for signed records, scoped by account/channel/genesis; it retains distinct signed authorizations, deduplicates equivalent ECDSA signatures by signed header/payload rather than signature bytes, maintains transactional capacity accounting, hides records after verified revocation, retains them for regrant, and prunes after local acceptance. It is not connected to the desktop or automatic gossip. Its forward helper does not yet enforce a final-transmit/chunk guard, so do not deploy it.

`authorized-pending-durable-store-r4.json` PASS13 three local Chromium profiles, actual authenticated c→b RTC with a fixture-installed receive handler: c signs a record, b verifies and stores it, duplicate and equivalent signatures are idempotent, concurrent capacity race preserves accounting, separate scope sees none, both c and b close, b reopens, a validator reopens, b explicitly forwards and verifies receipt, original enters accepted history once while c remains offline, store prunes accepted copy. `authorized-pending-other-author-r1.json` PASS14 additionally advances accepted history with a different author's message before forwarding; validator refreshes the unsigned witness and accepts c's still-valid signed authorization. `authorized-pending-store-revocation-r2.json` PASS12: author revocation hides/refuses the retained record, regrant restores visibility, but validator rejects stale authorization. `authorized-pending-offline-stale-r1.json` PASS9 proves even an unrelated permission change invalidates the author's global revision and validator correctly refuses it. Test fixture explicitly transfers/invokes/stores; no automatic product recovery, multi-validator or independent WAN. See `evidence/offline-author-recovery-design.md` for ordering, current revision limits, possible versioned per-author grant semantics and unresolved trust/security requirements. Next: final-transmit/chunk authorization guards, automatic signed-record creation/exchange/storage/retry with ordering and bounded resources, stale record behavior, stronger multi-partition tests; do not weaken existing validation to make this test pass.

### Source-only automatic offline-author signed handoff

`experimentalAuthorizedSharing` (default false, requires `experimentalPendingSharing`) now creates the consent-gated signed inbox and a separate background sender/forwarder in the normal channel session. It signs an ordered prefix of up to eight local pending originals and sends signed chat records to bound peers; readers retain verified authorizations and, when directly connected to a validator, try records matching their locally verified author sequence and permission revision. A verified receipt does not by itself replace history synchronization. The source exchange rechecks recipient read and author's write access on outgoing relay-submit control frames and chunks. This is not deployed or enabled on the live site.

`authorized-pending-runtime-gossip-r2.json` PASS13 and `authorized-pending-runtime-multiple-r1.json` PASS14 cover three local browser profiles with explicit RTC signaling: signed records are shared automatically, the author leaves, the reader restarts, the validator returns, and one/three messages are accepted exactly once. `authorized-pending-send-revocation-after-gossip-r1.json` PASS14 confirms the last-send guard after the sender learns revocation; `authorized-pending-legacy-coexistence-r2.json` PASS5 confirms ordinary unconfirmed sharing works when a simulated old peer rejects signed sharing and batches. `authorized-pending-offline-stale-after-gossip-r1.json` PASS9 confirms an unrelated permission revision invalidates an absent author's authorization; the current design must not claim it handles this case. Older manual tests additionally cover the chunk-send guard and another author's intervening accepted message. Tests are local, not independent WAN or multi-validator, and do not cover automatic validator-local submission, peer forwarding beyond a directly connected validator, all backlog sizes, or broad failure/pressure cases. See evidence/offline-author-recovery-design.md.

### Source-only signed message gossip across peers and local validators

The experimental signed inbox now gossips verified records between bound readers, not only directly from their author. It reuses the existing peer/author access checks at final transmission and per chunk. A local validator can also submit its own retained inbox records through the existing checked member submission and serialized round, after matching its accepted author sequence and revision. Original sending, peer copying and forwarding run in independently scheduled asynchronous tasks; these are not Web Workers. No live deployment or activation.

`authorized-pending-multihop-r2.json` PASS6: four local browsers and explicit RTC links, three messages pass from an author to one reader and then another after the author leaves; the first reader also leaves, the second restarts, then a returning validator accepts the messages exactly once. `authorized-pending-local-validator-r2.json` PASS5: the remote reader's relay submissions are deliberately rejected, and the validator submits three signed inbox records locally. `authorized-pending-lane-independence-r1.json` PASS5: one copied-record transmission is deliberately held open while another task forwards and accepts all three messages. These do not prove automatic peer discovery, real separate networks, consensus failover, unlimited queues or large scale; unchanged global permission revision can still invalidate an offline writer's authorization.

### Source-only pinned per-author authorization profile

`actor-epoch/1` is an explicit new channel-policy option, default absent. It is not installed or live and no existing channel is migrated. For chat only, the author's signed authorization binds its per-author epoch instead of the global permission revision; operation ID, author sequence, prior ID, signature, current write access and replay-set checks remain enforced. Initial public-write epoch is null; any permission event for that actor and block/unblock for the actor's bound account sets its epoch to the actual signed operation ID. Thus same-height differing permission events on forks cannot collide. Non-chat control operations keep global revision rules. Snapshot state includes sorted epochs only for the explicitly pinned policy. Existing policy shapes reject the new field on older clients; this has not yet been tested against an exact older packaged browser. Controller recovery is deliberately refused for this profile pending a safe authority-transition design. The change does not silently upgrade existing channels.

`actor-epoch-proof-r2.json` PASS82 covers independent witness oracle/quorum fixture and the new signed rule: unrelated permission changes, targeted revoke/regrant, bound account block/unblock, equal-height forks with distinct permission events, checkpoint round trip, invalid profile, and legacy signature rejection. `authorized-pending-actor-epoch-automatic-r2.json` PASS6 uses three local profiles and real explicitly signaled RTC: the sender leaves, a different actor's permission changes, and three saved records are automatically accepted once. `authorized-pending-actor-epoch-regrant-r2.json` PASS9 revokes and regrants the sender, observes twelve seconds with no old-signature acceptance, then shows the returning author signs anew and all messages converge. Earlier `authorized-pending-runtime-legacy-profile-after-epoch-r1.json` PASS14 demonstrates the legacy runtime; it predates the epoch token correction, which only changes the opt-in profile. No separate-network, mixed-version exact-package, multi-validator, recovery-handover, migration or large-backlog proof. More review and testing are required before activating a profile or declaring the larger objective complete.

## Recoverable controller experiment — 2026-10-29 UTC

Live release `native26-controller-backup-r1`, manifest `7034ae0e2f2c4e4b4ad8a04c7219835cc93b0fc0be4433da5b10d295d8878bbf`, managed config `3c60d408396e2c0b729b105ad0549d1e10a2ebd7a639d961008c92853ee30883`; previous release `native26-low-data-gossip-r1`. Normal replica journal refuses this controller for voting. This is an application guard, not proof that hostile same-origin signing code cannot manufacture a vote. Backups protect controller authority only: they do not restore validator keys, voting journals or quorum, and are not yet exposed as a user-facing backup/download workflow. No official channel has been permanently recovered or created. The API cannot back up existing nonextractable keys.

### Retained encrypted controller backup

Live `native26-controller-backup-retained-r1`, manifest `62a21519b39b17180d97d1a50d7c6de732809b37f2bc794d1b9dbdbf696007d9`, managed config `7ff5ac902d4dc8a0055103ded1c36ce9df3bfd894dbc078b29201f12e1839a8d`; prior controller-backup release remains rollback. Receipt `/srv/codi-connected/controller-backup-retained-activation-result.json`, renewal backup `/var/backups/codi-renew-before-controller-retained.service`. Recoverable controller creation and restoration now commit its encrypted backup to a separate bounded local IndexedDB store with strict durability before committing the nonextractable signing key; the view can retrieve the encrypted backup by scope and channel. If creation stops between the two commits, an encrypted orphan may remain; no key is committed before its backup. Existing controllers made before this release do not magically gain retained backups. Retention uses no server upload and is not a substitute for an external copy; browser-data clearing loses the local copy, and no user-facing download/restore flow exists yet. Wrong-scope lookup returns no record, conflicting retained backup is refused; records are bounded at 128 per account and 4096 per browser, and deletion/management UI is still missing. The validator and voting journal remain separate and unrecovered.

`.build/checks/controller-backup-retained-r2.json` PASS35 real Chrome includes page reload before export, scope isolation, wrong password/tampering and original custody checks; subsequent minor source ordering moved key validation before backup retention, with `.build/checks/controller-backup-peer-retained-r1.json` PASS4 against current source. `.build/checks/controller-backup-retained-live-r1.json` PASS6 uses three real live anonymous browsers: retrieval, unsafe validator refusal, wrong-password refusal, fresh-device restore, original browser closure, accepted message, and accepted spam mark. Same network only; does not prove crash/power-loss durability of both commits, independent WAN or complete channel recovery. Profiles and temporary upload removed. The earlier `.build/checks/controller-backup-live-r2.json` PASS5 proved restored moderation with the prior release.

### Account unblock observation and local cleanup

On live `native26-simple-chat-r1`, `.build/checks/registered-channel-unblock-observation-r1.json` exercised two registered test accounts and three browsers. The owner accepted a block; two enrolled devices each saved a message as pending while blocked; neither message appeared at the owner during the 10-second blocked observation. After the owner accepted unblock, both queued messages appeared automatically in accepted history. Test-owned accounts and browser profiles were removed. This is the current protocol behavior; it does not establish that all possible blocked attempts are refused permanently, and whether queued messages should be automatically retried after unblocking is awaiting user preference. Never describe this observation as a fixed moderation defect.

The user selected: messages attempted while blocked should remain unsent after unblock unless the sender chooses to resend. Work is source-only, NOT LIVE. `actor-epoch/2` opt-in binds an original chat proposal to the author's access epoch so a stale original cannot be made valid by silently refreshing its authorization; unrelated actors' access changes do not invalidate it. Existing channel policies remain unchanged and need an explicit migration/new policy; the current live system still automatically retries old pending after unblock. The access epoch also changes for permission changes, so an offline draft created before a later revoke/unblock may require review even if it was written before the block; without a trusted time source it is not safe to infer exactly when an offline draft was written.

### 512-block backfill and batch-size comparison

Current-source `.build/checks/member-512-gap-current-r1.json` PASS3 reused the private synthetic 512-block gap fixture with four local browsers, real RTC and one validator. The reader reconnected its older history to the unchanged accepted head in 253.638 seconds; 256 block-batch calls returned 512 block items, with 437 total instrumented member calls. Eight archive fill operations took 7.21 seconds aggregate; overlapping member calls totaled 386 seconds, so totals cannot be added as wall time. Profiles were removed. This does not measure independent Internet or 8,000 participants.

A local-only candidate requested two parallel groups of four instead of two groups of two. `.build/checks/member-bulk-four-legacy-r1.json` PASS5 verified fallback to an older provider; `.build/checks/member-bulk-four-multipath-r4.json` PASS34 checked two-provider concurrency, corruption rejection and access revocation. The first multipath fixture could not click newly nested controls; r2/r3 expected multiple ancestry pages even though all 18 certificates now fit in one; r4 checks all 18 and passes. `.build/checks/member-512-gap-bulk-four-r1.json` PASS3 completed the same gap in 250.648 seconds, with 145 bulk calls returning 484 items and 434 total member calls. The runs are uncontrolled single samples; this is not convincing proof of a speedup. In a separate eight-block diagnostic, two-item responses were 11.2–11.6 KB and took 161–405 ms; four-item responses were 22.7–23.2 KB and took 806–859 ms. Current inline values are limited to 12,288 bytes and larger values use chunked transport, a plausible contributor but not proven as the only cause.

The four-block experiment was NOT deployed. Working source was restored byte-for-byte to the prior two-block version; the exact trial source and its SHA256 are retained under private `.build/candidates/bulk-four-r1/`, and the prior live release remains `native26-listing-suppress-r1`. Next work should investigate transport sizing, negotiation, and per-phase timing before raising any wire limits; do not claim the desired seconds-scale catch-up has been achieved.

### Ten-browser accepted-message timing

`.build/checks/ten-chat-concurrent-latency-i36-live-r1.json` PASS6: ten browsers found and joined a live user channel, and all nine replies were observed as accepted by all ten windows. Concurrent observers measured 6.945–25.339 seconds from the sender action to the last accepted UI entry (median 12.638 s). The i36 browser was last for all nine samples, including its own message. The nine workstation windows observed the first eight messages within 1.659–10.885 seconds; the i36-sent message took 11.156–15.109 seconds in those windows. This suggests a Pi, remote-driver, or path-related bottleneck, but does not distinguish them. The timing includes UI, acceptance, WebDriver and scheduling; it is not wire latency. Reconnect assertions check displayed text rather than distinguishing accepted from pending. Nine samples on home-connected hosts do not establish independent-WAN behavior or general latency. The renderer JavaScript used heaps after the run were roughly 23–49 MB; these exclude browser-native memory and the guest, and were not measured after forced collection. All owned profiles and one test directory reference were removed; no accounts were created.

The receipt's inherited `scope` says three networks in error: nine browsers were local and one was on i36, all home-connected. The test scripts' descriptions were corrected after the run; the original receipt is preserved unchanged. `.build/checks/ten-chat-accepted-latency-i36-live-r1.json` also passed all nine accepted replies with sequential observation (5.933–22.051 s), while `.build/checks/ten-chat-latency-i36-live-r1.json` included pending/unconfirmed text and cannot establish acceptance. These are separate uncontrolled samples, not an A/B performance comparison.


### Browser-side timing versus test-controller delay

`.build/checks/ten-chat-clock-profile-i36-live-r1.json` PASS6 repeated the ten-browser live workflow with `Date.now()` recorded inside each browser at accepted-message observation. Clock offsets were estimated using the midpoint of the lowest of three command round trips; the i36 calibration RTT was 136.56 ms, so one-way uncertainty is material. The Pi observed the nine accepted messages after 7.167–18.807 seconds, and its controller received the results about 29–172 ms later by the estimated clocks. In this run the Pi was last in eight samples; one workstation browser was last in the other. Thus a multi-second remote WebDriver response delay alone does not explain the observed delay; the measurement still combines delivery, acceptance and UI rendering. The nine-message test does not isolate those phases, prove independent WAN, or benchmark higher scale. All owned profiles and one temporary public listing were removed; no accounts were created.


### Pending versus accepted presentation timing

`.build/checks/ten-chat-ui-stages-i36-live-r1.json` PASS6 traced the first UI appearance of each pending, unconfirmed and accepted reply in ten live browsers. Owner acceptance for the first eight replies appeared at 1.914–4.020 seconds; i36 acceptance for those replies appeared at 4.681–21.251 seconds. Four of those eight appeared first as unconfirmed on i36, at 3.073–11.171 seconds; their accepted displays followed 3.947–10.657 seconds later. Other replies first appeared accepted. The Pi's own message appeared pending at 3.347 seconds, was accepted in the owner's view at 8.363 seconds and appeared accepted on the Pi at 20.437 seconds. Observations involve event scheduling, browser clock calibration, display refresh, peer delivery and verification; they do not isolate the slow function. First appearance is not a direct packet-arrival measurement. i36 was on the same home infrastructure, not independent WAN. The local profiles and one temporary directory row were removed, with no account creation.

### Faster rotation among open channels

Live `native26-channel-schedule-r1`, manifest `f3327ba2f09bf8d87231889103e9d7975479ad6c97d9896b00b369e2030b0086`, config `ad2a172a5585e8a555ae0c381d9a7c3a0dd97f060c2629a6ce1ba550e8e37ab4`; immediate rollback `native26-channel-32-r1`, root-renew backup `/var/backups/codi-renew-before-channel-schedule.service`, activation receipt `/srv/codi-connected/channel-schedule-activation-result.json`. The discovery scheduler skips channels already holding two peers without consuming a five-second slot, performs at most one channel lookup per one-second tick, and uses a per-channel cooldown of max(5 seconds, 2 seconds per open channel). Failure retries after five seconds; loss from a previously healthy two-peer set and successful service reannouncement clear the relevant cooldown. Existing authenticated admission, permissions, connection bounds and server quotas remain. A single channel retains five-second retry. With 32 equally eligible channels, first sweep is about 32 seconds and per-channel repeat interval is 64 seconds; busy/outgoing signaling, outages, CPU scheduling and quotas can delay this. This raises potential lookup traffic compared with the former one-per-five-seconds schedule; no bandwidth guarantee or 8k proof.

`scripts/channel-discovery-schedule-check.mjs` PASS8 deterministically checks fairness, cooldown, healthy skip, single-channel retry, failure backoff, lost-neighbor eligibility and reannouncement reset. `.build/checks/channel-schedule-rotation-r1.json` PASS7 used the exact compiled discovery service, two local Chrome browsers, signed local WS introduction and RTC: a deliberately reset initial sweep covered 32 distinct successful signed lookups in 31.287 seconds, then the 32nd channel connected, exchanged verified messages and recovered after introduction restart and peer loss. Its `announcementRequests` field counts both tracked announcements and lookups; the harness label is corrected for future runs. Profile and 16 unique temporary directory references removed; post-cleanup count zero. No actual peer delivery on public 32-channel run, independent WAN, or large-channel proof. ### Live two-island pending/acceptance recovery

`.build/checks/channel-islands-live-r1.json` PASS8 used four disposable public HTTPS browsers: three on workstation and one on i36 (outbound 104.180.210.36), one public user-created channel, no accounts. After all joined and each intended pair had a ready RTC connection, test-only wrappers around each browser's `RTCDataChannel.send` silently dropped sends to the other pair while allowing sends to the paired participant. The owner was in the first pair and remained the channel's sole validator. In the split, the owner's group accepted its own message, the other pair exchanged two displayed pending/unconfirmed messages, and an eight-second observation saw no new cross-island messages; the two messages on the ownerless side were not shown as accepted. After filters were removed, every browser showed all three messages exactly once as accepted. The test checks displayed UI classification and cross-group absence, not an independently verified proof trace or arbitrary malicious branches. The filter drops RTC payloads, not full network infrastructure/signaling; transport sequence gaps can trigger normal reconnection. This is not two independent validator majorities, competing accepted heads, independent Internet, or larger-island proof. The 149.422-second total includes browser setup, joins, waiting during split, healing, checks and cleanup; it is not an isolated latency measure. All owned profiles and one temporary directory row removed. Live product code/config unchanged; full goal active.

### Updated scale target

User direction supersedes the older 8,000-participant target: focus on usable, resilient channels in the 32–128 participant range for now. The 128 introduction-socket cap is not proof of a 128-person channel; real chat delivery, recovery, bandwidth and memory still need tests at the target sizes, including independent Internet. Stop treating 8,000 as an active milestone. The rest of the channel, chess, moderation, storage and independent-network release goals remain active.

### Peer selection, split isolation and SYSTEM — 2026-10-29

The live connected release is `native26-system-channel-r2`, manifest `894b758887f3b426944e668c81e089377549011856a2a1452d78d13167ca6893`, config `cb47b2724af5f8b55d3fccfed7e0870d7fa2bbb9b858afe8276a27388765e7ef`, immediate rollback `native26-gossip-direction-r1`, root-renew backup `/var/backups/codi-renew-before-system-channel.service`, activation receipt `/srv/codi-connected/system-channel-activation-result.json`. `/desktop/` remains separate. The `codi-official.service` package is now `/srv/codi-connected/official-services/system-channel-r2`, manifest `04fd3157bf1fbd094a4324a9654868a76179879cb0d0a6cc4a12988946e18d4b`, unit SHA `1d6b0849fd416defba44da218525427f18022c46518f8e4cb4b19b335bf9824b`, unit rollback `/var/backups/codi-official-before-system.service`, activation receipt `/srv/codi-connected/system-official-activation-result.json`. Do not restore the old official service while relying on SYSTEM; it does not support its read-only policy or role endpoint. It remains an available recovery input.

SYSTEM is the operator-designated official channel `s-YPEQOsH_YaVOpn7k4hpwkkAvit0-1CS2mYesgUfIQ`, pinned genesis `sFVD26Rbx58sI7Ki1gglbLEcPaOSVWtYdIkFiAYe5TQ`. Its signed policy makes it publicly readable and only the owner can write by default. The server account `codi-official` owns the private owner key and identity metadata in `/var/lib/codi-official/state/`; these are private runtime state, never public assets or Git inputs. The shared official store keeps verified history. After persistent device storage is accepted, network startup automatically joins and keeps the channel open without a Chat window, retries an unavailable role lookup, and normal peer introductions/discovery spread verified history. Chat pins SYSTEM first and indicates when the user cannot post. Without storage consent SYSTEM participation is unavailable. The current operator interface is CLI, not a finished admin GUI. To post, send text on standard input to `ssh box-webhost 'sudo -n -u codi-official /srv/codi-connected/venvs/517179c/bin/python -I -B /srv/codi-connected/official-services/system-channel-r2/scripts/official-admin.py --state /var/lib/codi-official/state system-post'`; do not put the key in commands or public files. Signing and witness generation are serialized by a private lock; the registry independently verifies and atomically appends. This initial single-owner system has no provisioned off-host owner-key backup or multi-validator failover; loss of the key prevents further notices and must be addressed before treating it as disaster-resistant.
